title: Swaps, FX Instruments and Credit Derivatives
objectives: Describe a plain-vanilla interest rate swap and compute the fixed payer's net cash flows against a floating leg
Relate the par swap rate to expected future floating rates
Price an FX forward with covered interest parity and distinguish FX forwards from FX swaps and NDFs
Explain CDS mechanics: premium legs, credit events, recovery rates and payout
motivation: The largest derivatives on earth are not options on fancy stocks, they are swaps: agreements to exchange cash-flow streams. A corporation with floating-rate debt, an investor holding euro bonds, a bank holding credit risk, each can now trade its cash flows for someone else's with a single instrument. This lesson completes the instruments toolkit with the three biggest families: rate swaps, FX forwards and credit default swaps.

blocks.text: Interest rate swaps: exchanging two streams of interest

blocks.caption: Swaps price off the curve: move it and watch the floating leg reprice.

blocks.md: A **plain-vanilla interest rate swap** exchanges fixed-rate interest for floating-rate interest on a shared **notional**, and critically, the notional itself never changes hands; it only scales the payments. The party paying fixed and receiving floating profits when rates rise above the fixed rate and loses when they fall. Why would anyone do this? A company with floating-rate debt that fears rising rates pays fixed (locking its cost); a bank holding fixed-rate assets pays floating (hedging its funding mismatch).

blocks.title: A 2-year swap, notional 10,000,000: pay fixed 4.2% annual, receive 1-year floating
items: Year 2: floating resets to 4.6%. Receive 460,000; pay 420,000. Net: $+40{,}000$.
Cumulative over the two years: $-20{,}000 + 40{,}000 = +20{,}000$ for the fixed payer.
The asymmetry is the whole point: the floating leg *adapted* to the new rate year, the fixed leg never does.

blocks.md: What fixed rate makes the swap fair at inception? Approximately the average of the expected floating rates, since a fair swap's fixed leg must match the floating leg's expected value. If the 1-year rate today is 4.0% and the 1-year rate, one year forward, is 4.4%, the par swap rate is roughly $(4.0 + 4.4)/2 = 4.2\%$ - exactly our coupon. (A rigorous pricing discounts each leg's flows to zero value at inception using the yield curve from the bonds lesson; the averaging shortcut is accurate for simple level curves.) At inception the swap's value is zero for both sides; afterward, its value to the fixed payer moves like a long bond - up when rates fall, down when they rise.

blocks.text: FX instruments: spot, forwards and swaps

blocks.md: FX quotes give the price of one currency in another: EUR/USD 1.1000 means one euro costs \$1.10. **Spot** settles T+2 by convention. A **forward** locks an exchange rate for a future date, and its fair level is pure covered-interest arithmetic: borrow one currency, convert at spot, invest in the other, sell forward. No arbitrage forces:

blocks.caption: Covered interest parity: the forward rate follows the interest-rate differential, not a forecast.

blocks.title: EUR/USD 1-year forward: spot 1.1000, USD rate 5%, EUR rate 3%
items: The euro is at a *forward premium*: dollars are more expensive to hold (5% vs 3%), so forward euros cost more dollars.

Check: convert 1.1000 dollars to 1 euro, invest at 3% → 1.03 euros; selling forward at 1.1214 yields $1.03 \times 1.1214 = 1.1550$, exactly $1.1000 \times 1.05$ from the USD side. Both routes agree, no free lunch.

An **FX swap** bundles a spot trade with the reverse forward (the workhorse of short-term collateralised borrowing across currencies); **NDFs** settle in dollars against a fixing for currencies that cannot be delivered offshore.

blocks.text: Credit default swaps: trading default risk

blocks.md: A **credit default swap (CDS)** is insurance-like: the protection buyer pays a periodic **spread** (quoted in basis points per year on the notional) and, if a **credit event** occurs (bankruptcy, failure to pay, restructuring), receives compensation for the loss. Compensation equals notional minus recovery: payout $= \text{notional} \times (1 - R)$, where $R$ is the **recovery rate**, typically 40% in standard contracts, with cash settled against a post-event auction price.

blocks.title: Buying \$10m of protection at a 250 bp spread
items: Annual premium: $10{,}000{,}000 \times 0.0250 = $250{,}000$ per year (about \$62,500 per quarter).
Suppose a credit event occurs and the recovery rate is 40%.
Payout: $10{,}000{,}000 \times (1 - 0.40) = $6{,}000{,}000$, the buyer is made whole on the default loss.
Interpretation: 250 bp means the market prices roughly $0.025 / (1 - 0.40) \approx 4.2\%$ annualised default probability under simplifying assumptions.

blocks.title: CDS transfers risk; it does not remove it
blocks.md: The protection buyer now faces the *seller's* credit risk, precisely why centrally cleared CDS and margin rules grew after 2008. And a CDS can be bought without owning the bond (naked protection), which is why CDS volume can exceed bond volume and why basis (CDS spread minus bond spread) is a traded signal in its own right.

A final orientation: this lesson closes the instruments arc. Swaps repackage *interest-rate* exposure, FX forwards repackage *currency* exposure, CDS repackages *credit* exposure, all by exchanging cash-flow streams priced with the NPV and no-arbitrage tools you have now used three times. The options module ahead adds the one thing obligations cannot do: the *right, not the duty*, to transact.

guidedExercise.prompt: You pay fixed 4.2% on a 2-year swap with notional 10,000,000, receiving 1-year floating set at the start of each year. Year 1 floating fixes at 4.0%, year 2 at 4.6%. Compute each year's net cash flow for the fixed payer and the cumulative position. Then state who is better off if rates *fall* sharply in year 2 to 3.5% instead.
hints: Net = floating received − fixed paid, both scaled on notional.
The fixed leg never changes; only the floating leg adapts.
guidedExercise.solution: Year 1: $400{,}000 - 420{,}000 = -20{,}000$. Year 2: $460{,}000 - 420{,}000 = +40{,}000$. Cumulative $= +20{,}000$. If year 2's floating rate fixed at 3.5%: receive 350,000, pay 420,000 → $-70{,}000$ that year and $-90{,}000$ cumulative, the fixed payer is *hurt* by falling rates and would envy the floating receiver.

independentExercise.prompt: A fund buys \$5,000,000 of CDS protection on a corporate at a 300 bp spread for 5 years. A credit event occurs at the end of year 3 with a 25% recovery rate. (a) What is the fund's annual premium? (b) What payout does it receive at the credit event? (c) Compute total premiums paid and the fund's net position (undiscounted). (d) What payout would a 40% recovery have produced?
hints: Premiums accrue only for years elapsed before the event.
independentExercise.solution: (a) $5{,}000{,}000 \times 0.030 = \textbf{$150{,}000}$/yr. (b) $5{,}000{,}000 \times (1, 0.25) = \textbf{$3{,}750{,}000}$. (c) Premiums: $3 \times 150{,}000 = $450{,}000$; net $= 3{,}750{,}000, 450{,}000 = \textbf{+$3{,}300{,}000}$. (d) With 40% recovery: $5{,}000{,}000 \times 0.60 = $3{,}000{,}000$, lower recovery means higher payout, which is why recovery assumptions matter when pricing protection.

commonMistakes: Thinking the swap notional is exchanged, only interest (or rate differences) flows; notional is a scale factor.
Forgetting that a fixed payer *loses* when rates fall, not just profits when they rise.
Applying the FX forward formula backwards: the higher-rate currency is at a forward *discount*, the lower-rate currency at a premium.
Treating a CDS spread as default probability directly, it is the price of default risk per year, related to probability via $(1 - R)$, not equal to it.
realWorldApplication: Corporations hedge floating-rate debt with swaps; treasurers lock FX for future invoices with forwards; bond desks buy CDS protection as cheap downside insurance on credit portfolios, together these are the largest derivative markets by notional.
quantFinanceApplication: Swap books are priced leg-by-leg off the constructed yield curve; FX desks run covered-parity checks continuously; CDS-implied hazard rates are bootstrapped from spreads and recoveries, all standard quant-developer workloads built on this lesson's mechanics.
summary: A vanilla interest rate swap exchanges fixed for floating interest on a notional that never changes hands; the fixed payer above was $-20{,}000$ then $+40{,}000$.
The par swap rate ≈ average of expected floating rates: forwards 4.0% and 4.4% imply a fair fixed rate of 4.2%.
Covered interest parity: $F = S(1+r_d)/(1+r_f)$; EUR/USD 1.1000 with USD 5% / EUR 3% gives a 1-year forward of 1.1214, the higher-rate currency trades at a forward discount.
CDS: protection buyer pays spread × notional (250 bp on \$10m = \$250k/yr); on a credit event the payout is notional × (1 − recovery) = \$6m at 40% recovery.

quiz.prompt: A CDS covers a notional of 20,000,000 at a spread of 180 bp per year. What is the annual premium, in dollars?
quiz.explanation: $20{,}000{,}000 \times 0.0180 = $360{,}000$ per year, the price of protection is the spread times the notional.

quiz.prompt: In a plain-vanilla interest rate swap, what happens to the notional principal at maturity?
options: It is exchanged from the fixed payer to the floating payer
It is exchanged both ways, netting to zero
It is never exchanged, it only scales the interest payments
It is repaid with interest by the fixed payer
quiz.explanation: Vanilla swaps exchange *interest streams only*. The notional is a reference amount; exchanging it would turn the swap into a bond pair.

quiz.prompt: EUR/USD spot is 1.1000. USD 1-year rates are 5%, EUR rates 3%. What is the fair 1-year forward rate, to four decimals (e.g. 1.1214)?
quiz.explanation: $F = 1.1000 \times 1.05/1.03 = 1.1214$. EUR (the lower-rate currency) sits at a forward premium.

quiz.prompt: Which statements about FX forwards and swaps are true?
options: A forward locks an exchange rate today for a future value date
The forward rate is set by the interest-rate differential, not by a currency forecast
An FX swap combines a spot exchange with a reverse forward
A forward requires paying a premium at inception like an option
quiz.explanation: Forwards are obligations struck at covered-parity levels, with no premium at inception, only options carry premiums. FX swaps pair spot with the reverse forward for term funding.

quiz.prompt: What does this Python code print?
quiz.code:
spot, rd, rf = 1.1, 0.05, 0.03
fwd = spot * (1 + rd) / (1 + rf)
print(round(fwd, 4))
quiz.explanation: Covered interest parity: $1.1 \times 1.05/1.03 = 1.1214$, matching the lesson's EUR/USD example.

quiz.prompt: State the CDS payout formula at a credit event and explain in one sentence why the protection buyer still bears risk after buying protection.
quiz.modelAnswer: Payout = notional × (1 − recovery rate); the buyer still bears counterparty risk on the protection seller, who must be able to pay the claim at the credit event.
quiz.explanation: Protection replaces the reference credit's risk with the seller's risk, the post-2008 push toward central clearing and margin exists precisely to manage this substitution.

flashcards.back: Exchange fixed-rate for floating-rate interest on a notional that never changes hands; par rate ≈ average of expected floating rates over the tenor.
$F = S(1 + r_d)/(1 + r_f)$; EUR/USD 1.1000 with USD 5%, EUR 3% → $F = 1.1214$. Higher-rate currency: forward discount.
Payout $= \text{notional} \times (1 - R)$; \$10m notional at 40% recovery pays \$6m. Premium = notional × spread (250 bp → \$250k/yr on \$10m).
Paying fixed = long the swap = gains when rates rise, loses when rates fall; value behaves like a bond position. Zero value at inception if struck at par.
